observations:
Torah #228 is a very short teaching (five sentences) structured almost entirely as an eitza (cause-and-effect) chain rather than a web of bechina (shared-nature) equations. The chain runs: [God perceives a soul capable of bringing repentance and making converts] → [He arranges machlokes/controversy against that person] → [those who approach despite the controversy do so sincerely] → [genuine gerim can then be made]. The proof is the Midrash on Vayeshev: Jacob sought tranquility, immediately Joseph's anguish fell upon him — because Jacob was making gerim (bechinas megurai aviv), he could not have tranquility, which was the necessary condition for true converts.

There is only ONE explicit bechina statement in the entire text: Jacob's convert-making is called 'בְּחִינַת מְגוּרֵי אָבִיו'. This is a single pair, not a cluster of three or more independent concepts connected by bechina language. A package requires at minimum two or three bechina-connected nodes forming a meaningful thematic domain.

The key structural concepts — נְשָׁמָה (soul), גֵּרִים (converts), מַחֲלֹקֶת (controversy), שַׁלְוָה (tranquility), יַעֲקֹב, מְגוּרֵי אָבִיו — are not bound to each other through bechina equations in this text. They are linked causally (eitza). Consequently, no new packages can be proposed from this Torah's source text. The teaching is structurally monadic: a single insight about why a certain spiritual condition (machlokes) necessarily accompanies the mission of bringing souls to return and converting sincere gerim.
